cards.front: What is the order of the electromagnetic spectrum from longest to shortest wavelength?
cards.back: **Radio waves**, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays. The groups do not have sharp boundaries.
cards.hint: Start with the group used for broadcasting and work towards the most energetic group.

cards.front: How do electromagnetic waves compare with sound when travelling through a vacuum?
cards.back: **Electromagnetic waves** can travel through a vacuum, whereas sound cannot. All electromagnetic groups travel at the same speed in a vacuum.
cards.hint: Think about what the wave needs in order to travel.

cards.back: **Ionisation** happens when an atom or molecule gains or loses electrons and becomes charged. It can damage cells and DNA.
cards.hint: Think about what happens to the electrons in an atom.

cards.front: What is the wavelength of a wave?
cards.back: The **wavelength** is the distance between corresponding points on successive waves.
cards.hint: Think about which two points on the wave you would measure between.

cards.front: What is frequency in a wave?
cards.back: **Frequency** is the number of complete waves passing a point each second.
cards.hint: Think about what you would count and over what period.

cards.front: How does frequency change as wavelength decreases across the spectrum?
cards.hint: Think about the reverse relationship along the spectrum.

cards.front: What does it mean for a wave to be transverse?
cards.back: **Transverse waves** have oscillations perpendicular to their direction of travel.
cards.hint: Compare the direction of the oscillations with the direction the wave moves.

cards.front: A student says a shorter wavelength means a greater speed in a vacuum. Why is this wrong?
cards.back: All electromagnetic groups travel at the **same speed** in a vacuum, so wavelength does not change speed there.
cards.hint: Think about what all groups have in common in a vacuum.

cards.front: Why does clear glass let visible light through but absorb most ultraviolet?
cards.back: Different groups of electromagnetic waves **interact differently** with the same material. Visible light is transmitted by clear glass, while most ultraviolet is absorbed.
cards.hint: Consider how the wave and the material interact.

cards.front: What three things can happen when an electromagnetic wave meets a material?
cards.back: The wave can be **reflected**, absorbed or transmitted. Which one happens depends on both the wave and the material.

cards.front: How is information carried by an electromagnetic wave in communication?
cards.back: Information changes the transmitted wave in a **controlled way**. A receiver detects the changes and recovers the information.
cards.hint: Think about what the sender does to the wave.

cards.front: Which group of electromagnetic waves is used to heat food in a microwave oven?
cards.back: **Microwaves**. They also carry signals between mobile phones and nearby masts, and to and from satellites.
cards.hint: Think about how a kitchen appliance heats food differently from a hot surface.

cards.front: What harm can strong microwaves or infrared cause to body tissue?
cards.back: They cause **heating** of body tissue. Strong infrared can burn skin.
cards.hint: Think about the energy the wave transfers to the body.

cards.front: Why is it wrong to say that every electromagnetic wave causes ionisation?
cards.back: Microwaves and infrared mainly pose a **heating risk** at high intensities. Ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are the groups that can cause ionisation.
cards.hint: Compare the main risk from microwaves with the main risk from X-rays.
